en.title: Facebook or Online Shop Did Not Deliver Your Product
en.directAnswer: Save the order, page URL, payment proof, messages and promised delivery date. First ask the seller for delivery or a lawful refund. If the facts show a consumer-rights issue, use the official DNCRP route. If the account appears fake or the payment was obtained by deception, a fraud/cyber complaint may also be relevant.

atAGlance.whoFor: A buyer paid an online seller but did not receive the promised product.
atAGlance.legalBasis: Consumers’ Right Protection Act, 2009; DNCRP; Cyber Security Act, 2026 and other criminal law where fraud is alleged.
atAGlance.mainRule: Separate an ordinary delivery dispute from deliberate fraud. Do not label every late delivery as a crime.
atAGlance.updateStatus: Current cyber-law references must use the 2026 Act and July 2026 amendment.

en.lawMeaning: Separate an ordinary delivery dispute from deliberate fraud. Do not label every late delivery as a crime. This page gives a general route. A person’s exact rights can change because of facts, documents, deadlines, legal status, court orders or later amendments.
steps: Save the listing and seller profile.
Ask for a clear delivery/refund date.
If fraud indicators exist, preserve evidence for bank/MFS and police/cyber reporting.
evidence: Screenshots; profile URL; payment proof; courier details; chat; invoice; refund promise.
en.simpleExample: A Facebook page takes payment and then deletes the page. The buyer should save any cached links, transaction ID and chat before devices or accounts are changed.
commonMistakes: Common mistakes: sending NID/passwords to a fake refund agent..

whatIf.question: What if the seller is only late?
whatIf.answer: Give a clear written request first.

whatIf.question: What if payment was through MFS?
whatIf.answer: Contact the provider quickly where appropriate.

en.specialistTrigger: Large fraud; multiple victims; stolen identity; threats; payment account under another person.
